REUTERS/Christiana Botic By Siddharth Cavale Nov 15 (Reuters) – The asphalt tanker vessel that struck a docked paddlewheel cruise boat in the Mississippi River at New Orleans last week experienced a steering problem in which its rudder was stuck in one position, US transportation safety officials said on Sunday. The American ?Cruise Lines paddlewheeler American Heritage, with 190 people aboard, capsized at the dock. No one was killed in the collision on Friday. The Atlantic Asphalt tanker was headed upriver when it experienced a “steering casualty” in which its rudder stayed in a starboard position and the vessel veered toward the river’s east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum told a news conference in New Orleans. NTSB officials said they do not know what caused the steering problem. The tanker’s voyage-data recorder was recovered on Saturday. Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of data and began analyzing information that includes bridge audio, rudder angle, propulsion performance and vessel speed, Barnum said. Recorder data showed the asphalt tanker was traveling upriver on Friday near the Crescent City Connection Bridge at about 12:26 p.m. local time (1826 GMT), two minutes before the collision, when it experienced the steering issue, Barnum said. The cruise ship capsized in about 22 minutes, NTSB officials said on Sunday. As the American Heritage toppled over into the river after the impact, harbor personnel, firefighters and onlookers scrambled to pull passengers to safety. Read Also: American Heritage Captain, Crew and Tug Operators Hailed as Heroes After Mississippi River Capsizing Audio captured by the recorder included the vessel’s whistle, radio warnings and requests for assistance, as well as commands to deploy anchors and other emergency ship-handling orders, he added. Issues under investigation include whether the tanker’s anchors were deployed and, if so, at what depth, as well as interviews with crew members and passengers, officials said. Interviews with the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt are scheduled over the next week, NTSB officials said. The agency will release a preliminary report in about 30 days, the agency said. Under the revised arrangement, Izmit will remain the service’s only Turkish port of call, with connections to Constanta in Romania and Varna and Burgas in Bulgaria. The change reduces the service’s Turkish port coverage while maintaining its connections with the three Black Sea gateways. Akkon Lines introduced the Bulgaria Shuttle Service in March 2026, initially connecting Gemlik and Izmit with ports in Bulgaria and Romania. The latest adjustment removes Gemlik from the BSS rotation, although it does not indicate a wider withdrawal of Akkon Lines from the port. The effective date of the revised rotation and any changes to vessel deployment have not been specified. articles.title: Tankers: A Crude Correction, But Rates Remain Well Above Historical Levels
articles.summary: A combination of factors have forced the tanker market rates lower this past month, but they still remain quite elevated by historical standards. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “crude tanker freight rates have taken a beating this month albeit from unprecedented highs, with key benchmarks...
articles.body: Tankers: A Crude Correction, But Rates Remain Well Above Historical Levels in Hellenic Shipping News 16/11/2026 A combination of factors have forced the tanker market rates lower this past month, but they still remain quite elevated by historical standards. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “crude tanker freight rates have taken a beating this month albeit from unprecedented highs, with key benchmarks dropping more than 50%. The rout started following the Democratic wins in the midterm elections, whilst a more de-escalatory tone from President Trump shifted sentiment in financial and commodity markets. Given the surge in freight rates seen this year was not driven purely by quantifiable factors, it is easy to blame sentiment for the fall in tanker rates. Undoubtedly this was a major factor, but it is not the only influence driving rates lower”. According to Gibson, “in terms of risk premiums, the immediate danger involved in a Hormuz transit remains unchanged. However, paper markets are less fearful of the future. In the physical markets, refiners are less concerned about oil supply than they were a few months ago. Indeed, a recent JPMorgan reported pointed to a surplus of 1.1mbd in September, rising to 1.4mbd last month, alleviating the need to panic buy. The IEA placed the October surplus higher at 1.7mbd with softer demand also contributing to the stock build”. “Supply chains have also been adapting to the current status quo. Since Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline resumed flows in September, the market has kept a relatively steady trade pattern. This has allowed tanker positioning to adjust, with vessels increasingly repositioning East to capture higher Hormuz volumes. In recent weeks VLCC supply in the Middle East has risen sharply, prompting sharp corrections on Gulf of Oman freight rates. Suezmaxes and Aframaxes in the West have also seen very sharp corrections. Extremely elevated freight levels inevitably dampened cargo enquiry and prompted Europe to increase its intake of Saudi barrels from Sidi Kerir in recent weeks, at the expense of longer-haul trades, which ultimately increased tonnage availability”, the shipbroker added. Source: Gibson Shipbrokers Ltd Meanwhile, Gibson also noted that “the poor weather which helped boost inefficiencies for midsize tankers in October has subsided, whilst cargo volumes have started the month lower. Aframaxes have been impacted by rising supply, with over 115 vessels joining the fleet this year, either through LR2s switching to dirty or newbuildings being delivered. Suezmaxes have had 43 new deliveries for the year to date. 35 new VLCCs have joined the fleet while an ever-increasing number of older vessels with questionable trading history have joined the Hormuz shuttle fleet. As such vessel availability has improved almost everywhere with more coming”. “Falling crude prices further weighed on tanker rates. Though the two are not always correlated, with freight being such a high share of cargo value, falling flat prices have forced freight to adjust to keep trades workable. Earlier this year, it was often commodity prices which had to adjust to keep arbs open, now increasingly freight is doing the work. Ultimately refining margins were being squeezed, consumer demand was under pressure from high pump prices. As such, freight rates were unsustainably high. Something had to give”, the shipbroker noted. “However, looking ahead it is important to note that risk is still high, Iranian oil has all but disappeared from the market, Chinese imports have recovered to the highest level since March, flows through Hormuz remain robust (though under threat from persistent attacks), operational inefficiencies are high and global oil inventories need rebuilding. Lower freight rates will reopen trading opportunities, and the risk of renewed conflict cannot be worn out. Bad weather often drives volatility in Q4 and Q1. Most importantly, even after this month’s correction, freight rates and earnings in the crude sector remain exceptionally strong by historic standards and with no end in sight to the wars in the Gulf and Ukraine, geopolitics will continue to call the shots”, Gibson concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-11-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost
articles.summary: Countries are struggling to design rules to make shipping companies comply with a new bunker regulation designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a senior International Bunker Industry Association official said Nov. 12, as Washington leads opposition to financial punitive measures. articles.body: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Countries are struggling to design rules to make shipping companies comply with a new bunker regulation designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a senior International Bunker Industry Association official said Nov. 12, as Washington leads opposition to financial punitive measures. International Maritime Organization member states, having failed to adopt the Net-Zero Framework as scheduled in October 2025, are due to meet again between Nov. 23 and Dec. 4 to discuss the regulation. “People recognize that we need a GHG intensity marine fuel standard, and that is sort of generally agreed,” Edmund Hughes, IBIA’s representative to the UN agency, told Platts. “The sticking point is on the financial aspects.” In its current form, the framework is composed of GHG intensity thresholds for marine energy that tighten progressively over 2028-2035, and financial costs for shipping companies failing to meet the standards. But the US has fiercely opposed what it describes as “a global carbon tax” on shipping for the financial element, and a growing number of member states have proposed various revisions to the framework in bids to achieve a compromise. “That is where we have the trouble. Because, obviously, the member states haven’t been able to identify the best approach,” Hughes said on the sidelines of the IBIA Annual Convention 2026. Compliance mechanism Countries supporting the current net-zero framework have designed the financial element to promote the use of low-carbon marine fuels, which remain much more costly than conventional, oil-based fuels due to limited availability. October’s average delivered bunker costs for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil are $22.78 per gigajoule in Singapore, compared with $27/GJ for bioblend B24, $28.48/GJ for LNG, and $48.47/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator. “No shipping company is going to carry on buying more expensive fuel while their competitors are not,” Hughes said. “You need some way of closing that price gap.” The IBIA official said challenges lie ahead for member states on how to design an alternative compliance mechanism if the current net-zero framework is to be revised. Most Pacific Island states and EU member states are officially still supporting the current net-zero framework while the US and Middle Eastern states remain opposed to it. Japan, China, Norway and some major flag states have presented new ideas on compliance mechanisms. “If you have a technical standard, you have to find a way to comply with it,” Hughes said. “You can go through quite a few semantic gymnastics to try and get the agreement, and that’s often what’s done at international level in multilateral discussions.” Outlook IBIA, the world’s largest trade association representing bunker industry participants, including bunker traders and fuel suppliers, has been granted consultative status with the IMO and its representatives regularly participate in IMO meetings. “We recognize and value, as a sector, having global rules,” Hughes said. “That helps in all sorts of aspects in terms of understanding what the compliance requirements are, understanding what the market needs, what we need to provide in terms of fuels, and what people want to buy.” Going forward, Hughes said IMO member states may need to coalesce around a net-zero framework in a return to its tradition of consensus building so future implementation could be ensured globally. In April 2025, a total of 63 countries won a vote to approve the framework’s current text after the US withdrew from the negotiations. Later, 57 countries won another vote to delay its adoption in October 2025. “There was a vote… that already sent a clear signal that there was no consensus,” Hughes said. “The people who win a vote might think they won, but they [actually] lost.” Source: Platts 2026-11-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Dry Bulk Shipping: Capesizes Retain Positive Momentum in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Capesize The Capesize market maintained a positive trajectory throughout the week, with the Pacific emerging as the clear driver of overall gains. Despite some midweek volatility, improving miner demand and increasingly competitive fixing levels saw C5 recover strongly, climbing from $13.80 on Monday to $15.20 by Thursday, before easing back to $14.50–$14.60 towards the end of the week. Activity picked up considerably, particularly from Wednesday onwards, with both Port Hedland and Dampier miners covering multiple cargoes and operators increasingly willing to pay into the low-mid $15s. The Atlantic presented a more mixed picture. North Atlantic sentiment remained positive, supported by improving demand on the Transatlantic and Fronthaul routes, while the South Brazil and West Africa to China markets struggled to establish similar momentum. C3 levels softened as the week progressed, with fixtures slipping from around $36 to $35, reflecting limited index-date demand and a widening gap between bids and offers. Overall, the BCI 182 5TC built on its $40,000 level, reaching a high of $43,860 before closing the week at $42,798. Pacific strength and North Atlantic resilience ultimately outweighed continued pressure in the South Atlantic. Panamax-Kamsarmax The market delivered contrasting performances this week, with the Atlantic maintaining a firm tone while the Pacific struggled to gain momentum. Strong transatlantic demand and limited prompt tonnage supported rates, with an 82,000-dwt fixing around $18,000 for a US East Coast round trip and another at $22,250 basis South Africa for an East Coast South America transatlantic trip. Increasing North Continent tonnage availability offered charterers greater flexibility, while an 82,000-dwt secured $27,350 for a US Gulf fronthaul to China. East Coast South America remained supported by tighter early December tonnage, with an 83,000-dwt fixing at $18,750 plus $875,000 ballast bonus to the Far East and an 81,000-dwt at $18,500 basis retroactive East Coast India delivery. Meanwhile, growing Pacific tonnage availability outweighed Australian mineral demand, with an 82,000-dwt fixing at $22,500 early in the week compared with a 77,000-dwt at $19,000 towards the close. North Pacific and Indonesian activity remained subdued, with an 82,000-dwt fixing at $19,500 and a 76,000-dwt at $17,000 respectively. Period activity included an 83,000-dwt fixing five to seven months at $17,000 and an 81,000-dwt for one year at $18,000, both basis Pacific delivery. Ultramax/Supramax After declining for two weeks, the 11TC average showed positive returns in the second half of the week due to an improving Atlantic market. The North American market saw extremely limited tonnage for November dates, with transatlantic rates flying to new highs as a 63,000-dwt fixed for grains US Gulf to Continent/Mediterranean at $39,000 and a 64,000-dwt fixed for similar business at $40,000. A 61,000-dwt fixed petcoke to the East Mediterranean at $42,000, and a 64,000-dwt was said to have fixed on voyage on the same route in the mid $40,000s. There were modest gains in the South Atlantic, whilst the Continent and Mediterranean markets remained steady in light trading. Rates slowly softened in Asia as NoPac grains slowed, with a 64,000-dwt fixed for a round voyage at $21,000 and a 63,000-dwt concluded at $27,000 basis North China via NoPac to Bangladesh, whilst backhaul demand remained strong. Further south, the market was affected by a weak Indian Ocean market with ballasting tonnage competing for Indonesian stems, with larger units switching attention to Australian cargoes for better returns. With a falling spot market in the East, there was limited period activity, however a modern 63,000-dwt still managed to fix a strong $24,500 for 6 to 8 months basis delivery CJK. Handysize The week completed on a steady-to-firmer note, with sentiment largely positional across both basins. Across the Continent and Mediterranean, activity remained limited, although rates began to show signs of firmness towards the end of the week. The 37,000-dwt open Italy fixed for a trip to South Africa with charterers’ option WC India at low $20,000. The US Gulf and South Atlantic showed healthier momentum, supported by fresh demand and a balanced cargo-to-tonnage position, with a number of fixtures reported, particularly from the US Gulf. A 39,000-dwt open Mobile fixed for a trip to UK with pellets at $23,000, while a 37,000-dwt open Santos fixed via Brazil to Singapore–Japan range with parcels at $24,000. Across Asia, sentiment remained positive, with activity gaining pace and several fixtures concluded above previous levels, supported by a generally healthy balance between tonnage availability and cargo demand. A 40,000-dwt open Tomakomai 14-16 Nov fixed via Japan to Taiwan with slag at $19,500. Source: Baltic Exchange Tops 2026-11-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: VLCC Deliveries Rise Fivefold as the Orderbook Builds in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 VLCC supply is starting to arrive. After a sharp rise in ordering, the first of the new tonnage is reaching the water, with deliveries already well ahead of last year. Using VesselsValue data, we look at what is on order, who is building it, and why owners keep ordering at near-record prices. VLCC deliveries have moved significantly higher. There were just seven VLCCs delivered across the whole of 2025, while 35 have already delivered this year, five times the 2025 total. The pipeline behind them is substantial, with 349 VLCCs on order or launched, and the delivery schedule is heavily weighted to the next few years, with 125 due in 2028 and 113 in 2029. Overall, 27.3% of the VLCC fleet is on order. China sits at the centre of VLCC deliveries China holds 268 of the VLCCs on order, c.77% of the orderbook, and builds 106 of the 125 units, due in 2028. South Korea accounts for 59 and Japan for 15, so the build programme is firmly concentrated in one country. Our recent market chat on new and established yards entering the Tanker market looks at how this capacity is being added. Notable recent orders include three 320,000 DWT VLCCs ordered by Bahri, set to be built at International Maritime Industries (IMI) and set for delivery in 2029, contracted at USD 150.3 mil each en bloc, VV Value USD 127.69 mil. IMI is Saudi Arabia’s first large-scale shipbuilding project, and these are the only VLCCs on order at a Saudi yard. 219 VLCCs have been ordered this year to date, compared to just 85 in 2025, and newbuilding values have risen with it. Prices are up 15% year-on-year, from USD 125.59 mil to USD 144.51 mil, close to the all-time high of USD 154 mil in Oct 2008. Why demand is holding up despite high prices and a large orderbook Replacement alone does not explain it, as the 349 VLCCs on order or launched compares with 183 vessels aged 20 years and above. Tankers have been in short supply in recent years because of sanctions and geopolitics, and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz has tightened availability further. Earnings have reached levels that were previously unthinkable, which strengthens the case for newbuilding even at current prices. Middle Eastern producers are also a factor. With shipowners reluctant to transit the Strait of Hormuz since the disruption began, some producers have looked to buy or build their own VLCCs so that they have vessels available to move their crude whatever the conditions. This moves them from relying on the open market for tonnage to owning the capacity they need to get barrels out, and it adds a further source of newbuilding demand alongside strong earnings. The age profile shows where supply could be removed if conditions change. Of the 932 VLCCs in the fleet, 45.8% are 15 years or older, including 183 vessels aged 20 years and above. That leaves a sizeable pool of tonnage that could be considered for demolition should the market weaken. VLCC deliveries continue to build Taken together, the data points to a VLCC fleet that is about to grow at a pace not seen in recent years, with the build programme concentrated in China and delivery volumes weighted to 2028 and 2029. Demand for newbuildings has held up so far because earnings, tight tonnage availability, and energy security concerns have outweighed the cost of ordering at near-record prices. Should conditions change, the ageing fleet offers a sizeable pool of tonnage that could leave the market, so the balance between deliveries and demolition will be one to watch. articles.body: Australia Bauxite: Fewer Cargoes Overall, but More of Them Bound for China in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Lower exports overall. Signal Ocean’s tracked flows show Australian bauxite exports reached 51.44 Mt during January–October 2026, down 4.8% from 54.05 Mt a year earlier and slightly below the 51.73 Mt recorded in the same period of 2024. The decline was not uniform throughout the year. Q3 shipments increased 6.4% quarter-on-quarter to 17.08 Mt, although they remained 5.1% below the corresponding period of 2025. October exports reached 5.79 Mt, down 3.2% month-on-month but 1.3% higher year-on-year. China’s share of Australian bauxite exports has grown. Australian bauxite shipments to China increased 2.7% year-over-year to 36.41 Mt during January–October 2026, while exports to other destinations declined 19.1% to 15.03 Mt. articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: A drop in the tank in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Several producers are developing small-scale low- and zero-emission fuel projects around the world. But shipping needs far greater volumes available at competitive prices and at major bunker locations. Several small-scale biofuel and e-fuel projects are being developed around the world. Swiss startup Synhelion expects to start commercial operations at its 1,000 mt/year synthetic fuel plant in Germany in 2028. German-Brazilian startup Atlanteo is developing a modular e-methanol production concept, with its first 20 MW plant expected to produce around 10,000 mt/year. European Energy’s Kassø e-methanol facility in Aabenraa, Denmark, which is already operating, produced 4,974 mt of e-methanol in the first half of 2026, against a planned capacity of 32,000 mt/year. The company is also planning a 48,000 mt/year e-methanol plant in Québec, Canada, with Greenfield Global. ENGIE is planning a biomethane production facility at the HAROPA port complex in France, with an expected output of 7,000 mt/year intended for CMA CGM’s LNG-capable fleet. Smaller-capacity projects can help developers test technologies, identify production challenges and establish commercial supply chains. But proving a concept works is one thing. Making it work at scale to meet potential demand is another. A large ocean-going vessel can consume thousands of mt/year of fuel. That puts the output of a 1,000 mt/year plant into perspective. Even a 10,000 mt/year facility could typically serve only a limited number of vessels, depending on their size and fuel consumption. And shipping is hardly the only customer waiting at the door. A number of low- and zero-emission fuel producers are diversifying the allocations across multiple sectors, including aviation, road transport, chemicals and fertilisers, leaving several industries competing for the same molecules. Then comes the cost of getting that fuel to ships. Producing renewable fuel at a competitive price doesn’t automatically make it a viable marine fuel option. Transport, storage and physical delivery costs can push up the final bunker price, particularly when production facilities are located far from major bunkering ports. Longer transport distances could also increase associated emissions, potentially reducing the environmental benefits of switching to cleaner fuels. This is where the distinction between scaling production and scaling supply becomes important. Some developers intend to expand existing facilities, while others are pursuing networks of smaller plants. Atlanteo, for instance, plans to replicate its modular facilities in locations with suitable renewable energy and agricultural resources. Synhelion has outlined plans for larger plants in Germany and Morocco. Both approaches could increase production capacity. But the real commercial test is whether that fuel can reach ocean-going vessels in sufficient quantities without logistics costs undermining its appeal. None of this diminishes the importance of smaller projects. They provide an opportunity to test technologies and work through practical challenges before committing to larger investments. But a successful pilot is only the beginning. For renewable fuels to make a meaningful contribution to deep-sea shipping, producers must eventually develop supply chains capable of delivering sufficient volumes at workable prices to the ports where vessels actually bunker. In other alt fuels news this week, Frontier Fuels has chartered a barge for B100 deliveries on the Elbe, for supplying ships at five ports, including Hamburg and Cuxhaven. The barge, Lina, will carry only B100 (100% biofuel), the company said. It will also deliver to ships in Stade, Kiel and Brunsbüttel. The VO Chidambaranar (VOC) Port Authority will commence methanol bunkering at the port by the end of November. The port’s methanol bunker infrastructure comprises an onshore storage facility connected to a jetty through a 2.8-km pipeline for shore-to-ship fuel transfers. US LNG bunker supplier REV LNG completed an LNG bunkering operation for Siem Car Carriers’ vessel Aristotle, marking the first such operation at the Port of Davisville in Rhode Island. The truck-to-ship operation also marks the first LNG fuelling of a car carrier in the US Northeast, according to REV LNG. PowerCell will supply fuel cells for an ammonia power project in Norway. The system is designed to generate 700 kW of electricity for commercial ships and will be tested in Stord ahead of commissioning in early 2028. articles.body: Shandong Marine Corporation (SMC) has launched a new container shipping service connecting Rizhao in China’s Shandong Province with Incheon in South Korea, strengthening maritime links between the two countries. The new Rizhao–Incheon Express (RIX) commenced operations on 11 November 2026, offering two sailings per week with a single container vessel of approximately 1,100 TEU. The service operates on a direct rotation between Rizhao and Incheon, calling at Sun Kwang New Container Terminal (SNCT) at Incheon New Port. According to the Incheon Port Authority, the new connection is expected to reduce transportation times and logistics costs between southern Shandong Province and the Seoul metropolitan area. The port authority estimates that the route could generate approximately 120,000 TEU in additional annual container traffic. Rizhao is a major Chinese port serving industries including steel, petrochemicals and paper manufacturing. The new service adds another direct connection to Incheon’s existing container network with Shandong Province, which already includes Qingdao, Weihai, Yantai and Shidao. The introduction of RIX expands the range of regular maritime connections available to shippers moving cargo between eastern China and South Korea.

Last month, combined imports at the Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Long Beach came in at 1,000,500 TEUs, or 20-foot equivalent units, just off September’s all-time high. Compared to October last year, loaded import, export, and empty container volumes were up more than 20% at the Port of LA and more than 11% at the Port of Long Beach, according to data provided by the ports. Port of LA Executive Director Gene Seroka on Thursday attributed the sustained surge to changing trade policy and uncertainty along other global shipping routes, US consumer spending and retailers restocking inventory. Port of Long Beach CEO Noel Hacegaba said he expected elevated container volumes to continue through at least the beginning of next year as importers frontload goods before a US-China trade truce expires again in January. “We expect to be busy at least through the first month of the new year and possibly through the first quarter,” Hacegaba told Bloomberg last week, adding that cargo needed to supply the AI boom is among the growth drivers. Meanwhile, exports fell 7% in LA and 6% in Long Beach compared to last year. Empty containers moving through both ports were 26% and 13% higher, a sign that ocean carriers were repositioning equipment for more shipments coming from Asia. The import surge across several of the busiest US ports is expected to taper off through the end of the year before falling 3% in January compared to the year before, according to the National Retail Federation. “Numbers are still strong even as the season winds down,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF’s VP for supply chain and customs policy. Gold noted in a statement earlier this week that the high volumes have led to backups, especially for rail-bound cargo at the major West Coast ports. Gold also warned of potential disruption to operations at the Ports of LA and Long Beach if a union of security workers and their employers don’t come to an agreement before a Nov. 20 deadline. articles.summary: From tax reform and green bunkering to ship registration and a new partnership with Shanghai, the government in Hong Kong is pursuing an increasingly ambitious maritime strategy. articles.body: Greater China Hong Kong’s five-year clock Splash November 16, 2026 0 265 4 minutes read From tax reform and green bunkering to ship registration and a new partnership with Shanghai, the government in Hong Kong is pursuing an increasingly ambitious maritime strategy. The challenge is turning policy commitments into lasting commercial activity. The latest instalment from our new Hong Kong magazine, which is being distributed across the city’s maritime week. Hong Kong’s government is attempting something more ambitious than rescuing a declining container port. It wants to turn the territory into what it calls a “global maritime capital”, earning more from the financing, insuring, managing and fuelling of ships even if fewer containers cross its quays. That change in emphasis has gathered pace throughout 2026. February’s budget proposed fresh shipping incentives, June brought tax legislation, September produced Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan and October has already seen proposed regulatory changes for green bunkering and a new agreement with Shanghai. The latest move came on October 20, when transport and logistics secretary Mable Chan signed a “brother port” cooperation agreement with Shanghai. The two cities intend to coordinate liner services, intermodal logistics, green shipping and maritime professional services. The agreement is significant for a port that has struggled against mainland competition: Hong Kong’s strategy increasingly relies on partnership rather than attempting to regain its former position in the container rankings. The clearest statement of intent came in the 2026-2030 plan and chief executive John Lee’s September policy address. The administration has explicitly called for a transition from “volume to value”, setting targets to reduce emissions from Kwai Tsing’s container terminals by 30% from 2021 levels, establish five green energy corridors and have 7% of Hong Kong-registered ships take up green maritime fuels by 2030. Green bunkering offers the most visible evidence of policy being translated into operations. Hong Kong completed its first methanol bunkering operation in March, followed days later by methanol bunkering alongside container handling at Kwai Tsing. From June 16, vessels carrying, using or bunkering eligible alternative fuels became entitled to port dues reductions of 25% or 50%, while qualifying Hong Kong-registered green-fuel ships can claim HK$60,000 annually for three years. The budget earmarks HK$34m for the incentives. In October the government gazetted measures to expand sea room available for green-fuel bunkering from 645 hectares to 2,877 hectares, including seven new anchorages. This is the sort of unglamorous infrastructure reform that matters to owners and suppliers assessing whether vessels can bunker safely without upsetting schedules. Yet storage and supply remain unfinished business. The administration wants green-fuel storage facilities at Tsing Yi South, with planning procedures scheduled for 2027 and tenders in early 2028. It also intends to announce its first green energy corridor with a mainland city later this year, connecting Chinese fuel production with international shipping demand. A green-fuel trading platform and carbon-accounting framework are also being explored. “Owners will ultimately bunker where fuel is available safely, consistently and at a competitive delivered price,” says Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group. It is a reminder that incentives cannot substitute for dependable physical supply. Finance + Shipping agenda A second strand involves attracting commercial activity ashore. A bill gazetted in June seeks to improve shipping-related tax concessions, including adjustments to accommodate international minimum-tax rules, and introduce half-rate profits tax for qualifying physical commodity traders. The legislation remains before lawmakers in October. The rationale is that commodity trading produces demand for chartering, insurance, finance and maritime legal services. Simply offering lower tax rates to shipowners will not, by itself, rebuild that ecosystem. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, welcomes the administration’s proposed ‘Finance + Shipping’ agenda, which seeks to join ship finance, marine insurance and arbitration into a more compelling package. The government wants more underwriting capacity for specialist marine risks and is supporting the Hong Kong Shipowners Mutual Assurance Association’s development of international business, alongside promotion of the city’s arbitration services. But Hext offers a useful measure of success. “The next phase should be judged by substantive functions, regional headquarters, underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks and skilled jobs, and not by company registrations alone,” he says. Ship registration is another target. The government is preparing legislation to permit dual registration arrangements for bareboat-chartered ships, allowing owners to suspend one registration temporarily while a vessel operates under another flag. The objective is to make Hong Kong’s registry more useful to the increasingly complicated leasing and chartering structures of international fleets. The changes remain proposals rather than enacted reforms. At the port At the waterfront, the Port Community System launched in January to connect cargo information across sea, land and air. By September, more than 8,000 enterprises had registered and verified cargo data had supported more than 20 successful trade-finance applications. The next stage promises offshore cargo tracking using blockchain technology, while Kwai Tsing is earmarked for greater use of remotely operated cranes, autonomous electric vehicles and shore power. The city is also seeking new inland cargo through expanded rail-sea and river-sea links and deeper cooperation with Greater Bay Area ports. More direct liner connections to Central and South America are among the government’s priorities. Talent Then there is talent. Lee has proposed a maritime academy built around cooperation between educational institutions and employers, and the five-year plan calls for closer engagement with mainland training institutions and maritime technology researchers. “If I could choose one thing, it would be accelerating our maritime talent strategy,” says Angad Banga, chief executive of The Caravel Group. “Talent takes far longer to develop.” Promotion is part of the offensive too. The tenth Hong Kong Maritime Week takes place in November, with the government, shipowners and the International Chamber of Shipping bringing international executives together in the territory. The strategy is wide-ranging, but the industry still sees gaps in execution and governance. Horace Lo, group managing director of Modern Terminals, identifies “the establishment of a Maritime and Port Authority, and closer collaboration among ports in the GBA” as priorities. Others want faster progress on physical fuel storage and greater evidence that financing and insurance decisions are actually being made locally. Hong Kong now has a more detailed maritime programme than it has had for years. Its credibility will depend not on how many initiatives are announced, but on whether they bring cargo, capital, specialist jobs and commercial authority back to the city. articles.body: Americas Containers Dry Cargo Operations Regulatory Tankers US extends Jones Act waiver into February Adis Ajdin November 16, 2026 0 1,218 1 minute read White House White House Washington has extended its Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to continue competing for selected domestic cargo movements between US ports into February next year. The Department of Homeland Security approved the third extension of the waiver introduced in March, according to a November 13 notice from US Customs and Border Protection. The new period starts on November 16. Eligible cargo must be loaded before 11.59 pm Eastern Time on February 14, 2027. Foreign-flagged ships will still need individual approval before undertaking coastwise voyages. Cargo interests must submit vessel availability requests to the relevant US authorities, after which the Maritime Administration will survey the market to determine whether suitable Jones Act-qualified tonnage is available. The requirement keeps the tighter approval system introduced in August rather than restoring the broader exemptions available earlier in the year. The waiver was initially introduced in March amid disruption to US fuel supplies and shipping markets following the outbreak of war with Iran. It allows specified commodities to move between domestic ports aboard vessels that would ordinarily be barred from the trade under the Jones Act. The latest extension has drawn renewed criticism from the American Maritime Partnership, which represents US maritime interests and wants the exemption brought to an end. The group urged Washington to continue scrutinising individual applications, warning against allowing foreign vessels to displace American ships and crews on routine commercial movements. The Jones Act generally reserves domestic waterborne cargo movements for US-built, US-owned and US-flagged vessels meeting the law’s requirements. The extension leaves those restrictions in place outside the approved waiver arrangements. articles.title: India eases flag rules in push for more tonnage
articles.summary: India has relaxed its ship registration rules, allowing vessels with majority Indian ownership to qualify for the national flag in a move that opens the door to foreign minority investment. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has set the ownership threshold at more than 50%, replacing the full qualifying...
articles.body: Asia Operations Regulatory India eases flag rules in push for more tonnage Adis Ajdin November 16, 2026 0 378 1 minute read India has relaxed its ship registration rules, allowing vessels with majority Indian ownership to qualify for the national flag in a move that opens the door to foreign minority investment. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has set the ownership threshold at more than 50%, replacing the full qualifying Indian ownership requirement imposed under the previous Merchant Shipping Act. A government notification published in the Gazette of India sets out the new conditions under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. The threshold applies to legal ownership of shares in the vessel itself, rather than simply the shareholding of a company operating it. Eligible Indian interests can meet the requirement individually or collectively. Qualifying owners include Indian citizens, non-resident Indians, overseas citizens of India, Indian-incorporated companies, cooperatives and limited liability partnerships. Where a non-resident Indian or overseas citizen of India holds the majority interest, an authorised representative based or incorporated in India must be appointed. The change does not automatically give qualifying ships the right to fly the Indian flag. Owners should still complete the registration process and obtain approval from the authorities. The move comes during a wider push by New Delhi to increase Indian-flagged tonnage and strengthen its domestic shipping industry. Splash reported last year that MSC, Maersk and CMA CGM were looking to shift vessels onto the Indian register, while Hapag-Lloyd signed agreements with the government in March covering possible reflagging of up to four ships. India is also building out its state-backed Bharat Container Shipping Line and has launched initiatives targeting ship finance, insurance and domestic shipbuilding. Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout via REUTERS BUCHAREST, Nov 15 (Reuters) – Drones have struck three commercial ships in the Black Sea near Romania’s Sulina canal , Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Sunday, adding that his armed forces had scrambled fighter jets twice. Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said there were no casualties and that the ships’ crews had managed to control the fires on board after the strikes late on Saturday. A growing series of deadly strikes on merchant ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria shows how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for the transatlantic alliance in the Black Sea. The Sulina canal is a key Romanian shipping lane which links the Danube river to the Black Sea and is used by Ukraine for exports. Romanian officials did not identify the origin of the drones but said they were a direct consequence of Russia’s war in Ukraine . “These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said. “They reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.” Related Article: IMO Warns of Mounting Human Toll as Attacks on Commercial Shipping Continue Russia has denied targeting Ukraine’s neighbours with drones. Oprea said the three struck ships were Greek-flagged oil and chemical tanker Evia Petrol V, bulk carrier Marsol and oil products tanker Ali Najafov, both under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Evia Petrol V and Marsol were struck 4 and 5 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, the defence ministry said, inside Romanian territorial waters. Oprea said a separate general cargo ship was hit by a drone late on Friday, also with no casualties. Private television station Digi24 said the vessel was Palau-flagged general cargo ship Larissa 1. “On Tuesday and Wednesday I will be in Brussels for the meeting with my fellow (defence) ministers,” Oprea said. “We need the solidarity of our allies, shown through patrols with surveillance aircraft and through equipment for counter-drone warfare.” France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 maritime patrols aircraft to Romania after it asked for reinforcement. Many of the ships hit in October and November were anchored near or sailing to or from the Sulina canal . (Reporting by Luiza Ilie, Editing by Andrew Cawthorne) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.title: American Heritage Captain, Crew and Tug Operators Hailed as Heroes After Mississippi River Capsizing
articles.summary: The captain and crew of the American Heritage, along with tugboat operators and first responders who rushed to the scene, are being hailed as heroes following Friday’s dramatic collision on...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: Tow Boaters Facebook group The captain and crew of the American Heritage , along with tugboat operators and first responders who rushed to the scene, are being hailed as heroes following Friday’s dramatic collision on the Mississippi River that left the river cruise ship capsized but everyone aboard alive. American Cruise Lines singled out Captain Leonard Stewart, who remained on the bridge as the vessel overturned after being struck by the tanker Atlantic Asphalt at the Port of New Orleans on November 13. “The fast actions of Captain Leonard Stewart and our crew allowed for a rapid evacuation of the vessel,” the company said in a statement Saturday. “Captain Stewart remained on the bridge as the vessel capsized, calling for aid and keeping the ship alongside the dock for as long as possible.” The collision occurred at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time, just below the Crescent City Connection bridge. The impact caused the American Heritage to take on water and eventually roll onto its side, sending passengers and crew into the Mississippi River. As the riverboat began to capsize, help arrived from nearly every direction. Harbor tugs, towboats and other working vessels raced toward the scene, joining the U.S. Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans Harbor Police, New Orleans Fire Department and other emergency responders in a massive rescue operation. AIS data and local reports showed crews from Moran Towing, Crescent Towing, Cooper Mooring, John W. Stone Oil Distributor and Canal Barge Co. responding within minutes of the collision. Among the vessels identified near the scene were Moran’s Becky S , Crescent Towing’s Mardi Gras and G. Shelby Friedrichs , the E.N. Bisso tug Marauder , and several Stone Oil towboats, including Presager , Madison Stone , Stephanie Stone and Stone Power . Canal Barge’s Elly Lane was also among the vessels identified, along with the Port of New Orleans fireboat Gen. Roy S. Kelley . While AIS positions alone do not establish the specific actions taken by every vessel, footage and accounts from the scene show working boats joining emergency craft in the rescue effort. Captain Kenny Brown of The Maritime Throwdown praised the private-sector crews whose contributions can sometimes be overlooked amid the attention given to government emergency responders. “When something goes wrong on the river, the first boats you usually see on scene are towboats and tugs,” Brown wrote. “Nobody calls them in. They’re already there, and they turn toward the trouble.” Brown credited the captains, pilots and deckhands who maneuvered their vessels into position and helped with the response. “To the captains who made the call, the pilots who held those boats steady, and the deckhands out on the deck with life rings and pike poles in hand: that’s courage, and the river saw it.” The response was extraordinary in its speed and scale. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said 87 passengers and crew members were able to disembark before the American Heritage capsized. It then took approximately 30 to 45 minutes for rescuers to pull the remaining people from the river and account for everyone. Mayor Helena Moreno described the outcome as a “miracle on the Mississippi,” crediting the coordinated efforts of government responders and nearby vessels that voluntarily joined the rescue. All passengers and crew were accounted for, with no fatalities. Thirty-two people, including two Harbor Police officers, were transported to hospitals. Eight remained hospitalized as of Saturday, according to local officials. American Cruise Lines thanked the Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans, New Orleans Police Department and other agencies involved in the response. “We are proud of our crew and grateful for the first responders,” the company said, adding that it would continue cooperating with authorities through the investigation and salvage effort. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the collision, including reports that the Atlantic Asphalt may have experienced a steering failure before striking the docked riverboat. The cause has not been determined. The American Heritage remains partially submerged alongside the riverfront, with salvage operations expected to take weeks. For Brown, the incident also underscored the importance of maritime safety training, emergency drills and the ability to respond instinctively when seconds matter. “Practice until it’s muscle memory,” he wrote. “You don’t rise to the occasion. You fall back on your training.” The outcome in New Orleans was a reminder of the professionalism found across the maritime industry, from passenger vessel crews to the working mariners aboard the tugs and towboats that keep the Mississippi River moving. articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) covering shipments from the Far East to South Africa and from Europe and the Mediterranean to Latin America and the Caribbean, with implementation dates in November and December 2026. The French container shipping company will introduce a surcharge of US$650 per TEU on shipments from the Far East to South Africa, effective from 15 November 2026. The measure applies to all cargo types and will remain in place until further notice. The surcharge will be determined by the loading date and covers cargo originating from Far East ports and destined for South Africa. New surcharges from Europe and Mediterranean to the Americas In a separate announcement, CMA CGM confirmed additional Peak Season Surcharges (PSS 02) on shipments from Northern Europe, the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea to destinations across Latin America and the Caribbean. The new charges will take effect on 7 December 2026, based on the loading date, and will remain applicable until further notice. All three measures apply exclusively to short-term contracts and cover all cargo types. For shipments originating in Northern Europe, excluding Portugal, and destined for the west coast of South America, the carrier will apply a surcharge of €200 per unit. A surcharge of €200 per unit will also apply to shipments originating from Mediterranean ports in Spain, Italy and France, as well as the Adriatic and Portugal. The measure covers destinations on the west coast of South America, the west coasts of Central America and Mexico, the east coast of Central America and the Caribbean, excluding the French West Indies. It also covers the Leeward Islands, excluding Gustavia and Philipsburg, and the Windward Islands. For shipments originating from the Eastern Mediterranean, Adriatic, North Africa and Black Sea, CMA CGM has announced a surcharge of US$200 per unit. This measure applies to the same destination regions, including the west coast of South America, the west coasts of Central America and Mexico, the east coast of Central America and the Caribbean, subject to the stated exclusions for the French West Indies, Gustavia and Philipsburg. The December surcharges will apply in addition to the carrier’s existing freight charges under the relevant contract terms. CMA CGM has not specified an expiry date for either announcement, with both measures remaining in effect until further notice.

The arrangement will give Yang Ming access to both Alexandria’s Old Port and El Dekheila facilities, alongside the container gateways of Port Said and Damietta. Through the slot-sharing agreement, Yang Ming will be able to market additional container transport connections within Egypt without directly operating the vessels assigned to the services.

articles.body: According to data from the US Census Bureau, the still-ongoing 2026 Transpacific container shipping peak season is not being driven by the boom in investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and is instead being actively fuelled by traditional consumer goods. Figure 1 shows the monthly Asia to US containerized imports in Metric Tons for January 2022 to September 2026, broken down into seven major categories. We mapped all HS8 codes in the data to five traditional container goods classification groups (A‑E) and created two new groups (F‑G). We do not claim that all goods transported under the F-G classifications are being used to build AI data centres, but that they could conceivably be contributing to it. Source: Sea-Intelligence.com, Sunday Spotlight, issue 790 The data shows that high‑value AI computer chips and IT equipment does not travel by ocean freight and is almost exclusively shipped by airfreight. Furthermore, when looking at the physical materials needed to build these massive data centres, the numbers show no significant impact on Asia-US volumes. The data shows that the import weight for data centre construction materials and infrastructure has remained almost completely flat. If the AI boom were truly driving Transpacific container volumes, we would expect to see an increase here. So, what is driving Transpacific volumes then? The 2026 peak season boom is being driven almost entirely by traditional container goods and raw manufacturing materials. We are seeing strong growth in the import of everyday consumer items like apparel, toys, games, sporting goods, and bicycles. Additionally, there are major increases in raw materials and intermediate goods like plastics, paper, packaging, and everyday hardware.

articles.title: Liquefied biogas storage tank installed at the port of Gothenburg
articles.summary: Construction of the biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg has reached an important milestone with the installation of the facility’s liquefied biogas storage tank. The plant is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027 and is expected to make Swedish biogas more accessible to more sectors,...
articles.body: Construction of the biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg has reached an important milestone with the installation of the facility’s liquefied biogas storage tank. The plant is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027 and is expected to make Swedish biogas more accessible to more sectors, not least shipping. LBG is a renewable, low-climate-impact fuel that can replace fossil alternatives, and interest in it is growing rapidly in the shipping sector. Groundworks, including foundations and base slabs, are complete, and the tank is the first of the plant’s key components to be installed. It arrived at the port by vessel, has a volume of 500 cubic metres, weighs close to 140 tonnes and will be able to store up to 200 tonnes of LBG once the facility is operational. Once finished, the plant will be able to deliver 250 gigawatt-hours of LBG a year, equivalent to the consumption of 500 trucks or the bunkering of 50 vessels. It will be the first liquefaction plant in Sweden connected directly to the west Swedish gas grid, creating a new market for Swedish biogas producers that are, or want to become, connected to the grid. Producers and users are already present at the port: ST1 Biokraft has signed an agreement securing part of the plant’s capacity, and several shipping companies that call regularly already use LBG to power their vessels. Therese Jällbrink, Head of Renewable Energy at the Port of Gothenburg, said shipping’s transition requires a collaborative value chain, that the facility strengthens the port’s position in renewable bunker fuels and allows LBG to be offered to shipping on a larger scale, and that the growing number of vessels on order for LBG operation points to strong potential for increased bunkering. Carolina Wistén, Head of Customer and Market, Gas Grid, at Nordion Energi, said the facility is starting to take shape and brings the goal of delivering LBG from the gas grid to shipping, heavy transport and industry closer.

articles.body: Americas Operations Tankers US court orders arrest of tanker after New Orleans cruise ship collision Grant Rowles November 15, 2026 5 70,947 1 minute read US Coast Guard Heartland US Coast Guard Heartland A US federal court has authorised the arrest of the tanker Atlantic Asphalt after the Port of New Orleans launched legal action seeking more than $1m in damages following the collision that sank American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage. The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans filed the lawsuit in the Eastern District of Louisiana, naming the tanker, its owner Nave Shipping SA and OSM Thome’s Singapore-based Thome Ship Management as defendants. The port has also sought the vessel’s sale to recover damages. The 17,764 dwt asphalt tanker struck American Heritage on November 13 , causing the river cruise ship to capsize and partially sink. Thirty-two people were taken to hospital following the incident, with no fatalities reported. The lawsuit alleges negligence by the tanker interests, although the cause of the collision remains under investigation. OSM Thome confirmed that it manages Atlantic Asphalt and said the vessel was stable at anchor following the incident. Dlouhy Nov 14, 2026 (Bloomberg) –President Donald Trump is giving energy companies and traders more time to transport oil and other commodities around the US on foreign-flagged ships, renewing a policy intended to lower fuel costs. Trump has decided to extend by 90 days a waiver of mandates under the century-old Jones Act that otherwise require cargo carried between US ports to be transported on American-owned, -flagged and -operated vessels, according to a White House official speaking on condition of anonymity before the decision is public. The extension comes just two days before a previous waiver was set to expire. It will take effect at 12 a.m. Monday New York time, ensuring no gap between the expiration of the prior one, the official said. The decision underscores the administration’s continued concerns about high energy costs due to the war in Iran , after Democrats trounced Republicans in the November midterm elections that were dominated by voter concerns about the cost of living. Trump did not change the breadth of the relief, after previously narrowing the waiver’s scope in August to require the government conduct case-by-case reviews of vessel availability. Read more: Maritime Industry Urges Trump to Let Jones Act Waiver Expire November 15 Shipbuilders and their allies on Capitol Hill had argued against any extension , saying they have undercut longstanding protectionist mandates they see as critical to bolstering domestic shipbuilding capacity. But oil and chemical companies said the waiver has helped move cargoes of crude, fertilizer and other commodities between US ports efficiently and at lower cost, helping counteract supply disruptions stoked by the war in Iran and refinery damage in Russia. Some 338 voyages have taken place on foreign vessels since Trump first waived Jones Act restrictions in March , including shipments of Texas crude to Pennsylvania and propane to Puerto Rico, according to government data analyzed by the Cato Institute. California has received the majority of shipments, with 23 million barrels of additional products carried to the state compared with 8 million barrels during the same period last year, the White House official said. An additional 90 million barrels of products — mostly refined fuels — have been shipped between US ports since the waiver was first issued, with gasoline, crude oil and renewable fuel being the biggest beneficiaries, according to the official. The current waiver has helped enable the transport of some 13 million barrels of products, more than a third of which has been gasoline, with about 28% crude oil. The waiver’s use, however, has shrunk after Trump limited its scope. Under the new approach, the US Maritime Administration needs to be consulted on the availability of US-flagged, -owned and -operated vessels before the waiver is applied to individual voyages. Products that benefit under the waiver include gasoline, jet fuel, crude oil, naphtha, liquefied natural gas, soy oil and fertilizers. Trump’s Jones Act exemption has been the longest and broadest waiver of the law in more than seven decades. Previous presidents have discretely lifted Jones Act mandates for individual voyages and short periods in the wake of hurricanes and pipeline outages that disrupted fuel flows. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Christiana Botic TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY All passengers and crew aboard an American Cruise Lines riverboat survived after a Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker struck the docked paddle-wheeler on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, causing it to capsize and sending people into the water. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed that everyone aboard the American Heritage had been accounted for following a massive rescue operation. Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals, including 30 passengers and two police officers, but none suffered critical injuries. “We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said at a news conference. The 160-meter tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the U.S.-flagged American Heritage at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time as it was traveling upbound on the Lower Mississippi River, just below the Crescent City Connection bridge, according to the Port of New Orleans. Video of the collision shows the much larger tanker striking the docked paddlewheeler, which began taking on water and listing heavily before eventually capsizing alongside the dock. Other footage shows people in the river wearing life jackets as tugboat operators, nearby vessel crews, police and emergency responders rushed to pull them to safety. The American Heritage had docked outside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building approximately two hours earlier to begin disembarking passengers following an eight-day Mississippi River cruise. Port officials initially reported approximately 129 passengers aboard, in addition to crew members. Moreno said passengers began evacuating after the initial impact, but the vessel overturned before everyone could get off, forcing rescuers to pull people from the water. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry praised the response, calling the outcome “nothing short of a miracle.” “While we will continue to work through the details of this incident, one thing is clear: our first responders on the national, state, and local level saved countless lives today, and for that I and all of our country are thankful!” Landry said. In an updated statement Friday, American Cruise Lines said it was arranging hotel accommodations and assistance for everyone who had been aboard the American Heritage . “We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need,” the company said. American Cruise Lines also thanked the U.S. Coast Guard, its crew and local first responders for their rescue efforts, adding that it remained in close contact with the Coast Guard, New Orleans Police and other agencies. The cause of the collision remains under investigation, although the U.S. Coast Guard said the tanker may have experienced a steering failure. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker appeared to have experienced “some type of loss of steering,” but emphasized that the exact cause had not been determined. The National Transportation Safety Board has launched an investigation and is sending a team to New Orleans, with investigators expected to arrive Saturday morning. The Coast Guard also closed the Mississippi River to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while emergency operations continued, temporarily disrupting navigation along one of the nation’s busiest commercial waterways. Officials said they were evaluating when the waterway could safely reopen. According to MarineTraffic , the Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-meter asphalt and bitumen tanker sailing under the Marshall Islands flag. The American Heritage is an 81-meter U.S.-flagged paddlewheel cruise ship built in 2015 with accommodations for up to 150 passengers. AIS data shows the Atlantic Asphalt called at Amuay, Venezuela, in October before arriving in Paulsboro, New Jersey. The tanker departed Paulsboro on October 26 and arrived in New Orleans on November 11, two days before the collision. The investigation will focus on what caused the tanker to strike the docked passenger vessel along the busy Lower Mississippi River, where deep-draft oceangoing ships regularly navigate in close proximity to river cruise vessels, tugs and barges. This is a developing story. Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: Tow Boaters Facebook group Update: ‘Miracle on the Mississippi’: All Accounted For After Tanker Capsizes Cruise Ship in New Orleans A Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker struck the docked American Cruise Lines riverboat American Heritage on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, sending people into the water and leaving the cruise ship capsized at the dock. The 160-meter tanker Atlantic Asphalt collided with the U.S.-flagged American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. local time below the Crescent City Connection bridge, according to the Port of New Orleans. Video of the incident shows the tanker striking the port side of the docked river cruise ship. In the aftermath, the American Heritage took on water, rolled over and subsequently capsized alongside the dock. Other video circulating online showed people in the water wearing life jackets as rescuers responded. Port NOLA said about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision. The mayor’s office said multiple people had been rescued and search-and-rescue operations were ongoing. American Cruise Lines confirmed that the American Heritage was involved in a collision while it was docked in New Orleans. “We are in close coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard and local authorities. Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved. We will share more information as it becomes available,” the company said. The collision triggered a major emergency response involving the U.S. Coast Guard, New Orleans Fire Department, police, EMS and Port NOLA Harbor Police. The Coast Guard has closed the river to all vessel traffic between mile marker 93 and 96 while responders assess the situation and conduct response operations. The NTSB is launching a “go team” to investigate the collision. The team expects to arrive tomorrow morning. According to vessel-tracking data from MarineTraffic, the 81-meter American Heritage had arrived from Natchez, Mississippi and docked in New Orleans earlier on Friday. MarineTraffic recorded a “proximity event” involving the Atlantic Asphalt at 18:29 UTC, or 12:29 p.m. local time, corresponding with the reported time of the collision. AIS data shows the Atlantic Asphalt called at Amuay, Venezuela, in mid-October before arriving in Paulsboro, New Jersey, on October 24. The tanker departed Paulsboro on October 26 and arrived in New Orleans on November 11, two days before the collision. The Atlantic Asphalt was not operating under the current Jones Act waiver, as it was continuing an international voyage after discharging part of its foreign-loaded cargo in New Jersey rather than transporting cargo loaded at Paulsboro to New Orleans. The Trump administration’s emergency Jones Act waiver, which was extended Friday, allows certain foreign-flagged vessels to transport domestic cargo between U.S. ports. American Cruise Lines said guests and crew had been evacuated and that it was coordinating with the Coast Guard and local authorities. Passengers were being taken to the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for assistance and medical evaluation. The cause of the collision remains under investigation. Authorities have not said whether the tanker experienced a mechanical or propulsion failure before the impact. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he had been briefed on the incident and was in contact with local officials as the emergency response continued. The American Heritage, built in 2015, is a 150-passenger paddlewheel river cruise ship operated by American Cruise Lines. The vessel features multiple passenger decks, private balcony accommodations and a traditional stern paddlewheel design. It operates cruises along the Mississippi River and other U.S. inland waterways. This is a developing story and will be updated. articles.title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
articles.summary: Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is...
articles.body: Containers Contributions From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 14,755 3 minutes read Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida , to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. The sinking of the SS United States reminds us that ships can outlive their commercial purpose. Launched in 1951 and entering service in 1952, the SS United States was the pinnacle of post-war American maritime engineering. It held the record as the world’s fastest passenger ship but was withdrawn in 1969 as commercial aviation transformed the economics of transatlantic travel. It was not poor engineering that made the ship obsolete, it was a market that had moved on. After decades moored in Philadelphia, the vessel was acquired by Okaloosa County in a project valued at approximately $13m. Its new role will support tourism, marine conservation and research. Its retirement offers a useful perspective on container shipping as it now faces another turning point. A substantial wave of new capacity The container shipping industry is preparing for a significant increase in fleet capacity. According to Drewry’s third-quarter 2026 Container Forecaster the global containership orderbook stood at approximately 13.9m teu on 1 September 2026, equivalent to 40.9% of the active fleet. Drewry forecasts fleet growth of 8.4% in 2027, rising to 12.1% in 2028 before moderating to 9.4% in 2029. The concern is the market into which these ships will be delivered. During the pandemic, congestion, equipment shortages and route disruption absorbed vessel capacity. Diversions around the Cape of Good Hope lengthened voyages and tied up ships. Carriers responded by ordering larger, more fuel-efficient vessels anticipating continued trade growth, but shipbuilding schedules are long and in the era of the never normal, market conditions change quickly. If Red Sea and Suez Canal routings return progressively to normal, shorter voyages could release significant effective capacity without a single additional ship entering service. Combined with newbuildings, this could widen the gap between supply and demand. Vessel capacity could potentially reach as much as 10% above demand under such circumstances. The consequences could include lower freight rates, tougher competition for cargo, blank sailings, slower steaming, vessel idling and accelerated recycling of older tonnage. The industry faces a major capacity-management challenge. The cost of getting the timing wrong Aviation permanently changed the market for passenger liners, while container shipping remains essential to trade. New vessels will not automatically become redundant. Nevertheless, ships are long-term capital investments, ordered years before delivery and expected to earn returns over operating lives spanning decades. A vessel ordered when freight rates are high and capacity constrained may enter service when demand is weaker, transit times are shorter and competing tonnage is plentiful. Efficiency alone cannot guarantee a satisfactory return. Carriers will have to decide which vessels to deploy, which trades to prioritise and when to redeploy or retire older ships. Smaller vessels displaced from mainline routes may move into regional trades, adding competitive pressure whilst others may be laid up, sold or recycled. Ports and terminals may see service patterns, berth requirements and transhipment flows change. Shippers may welcome lower rates but carriers protecting utilisation may consolidate services, withdraw sailings or alter port rotations. Lower prices could therefore come with less predictable frequency and transit times. The costs of poor capacity planning will ultimately ripple through businesses to end users and consumers. A different future for ageing vessels The SS United States project raises the question of what happens when ships lose their original commercial purpose. Conversion into an artificial reef offers a potential tourism and conservation role but it is neither a universal nor necessarily economical solution for commercial vessels. For surplus container ships, recycling will remain the principal end-of-life option when redeployment is no longer viable. Some older vessels may serve feeder networks or specialised trades, provided their economics remain competitive. Fleet renewal should consider the economic, environmental and operational consequences of retiring existing tonnage and not just the efficiency gains promised by newbuildings. The SS United States was a remarkable engineering achievement but it could not escape changing transportation economics. Its story reminds us that a ship’s commercial lifespan is determined not simply by how well it is built but by whether the market still needs what it does. As the industry approaches 2027, the question is whether carriers have ordered more capacity than the market can sustainably absorb and how prepared they are to manage the consequences. The challenge is not simply to build the next generation of vessels. It is to ensure there is a commercially sustainable reason to put them to work. It’s not something we as an industry have a good track doing. The New York- and Oslo-listed gas carrier giant has agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,134 cu m BW Mistral , with the transaction expected to generate a net book gain of around $37m and net cash proceeds of approximately $104m. The buyer has not been disclosed. Built at China’s Jiangnan shipyard, the scrubber-fitted vessel is currently trading in the spot market and will continue earning revenue for BW LPG until its scheduled handover by mid-January 2027. Chief executive Kristian Sørensen said the ship had contributed significantly to earnings since joining the fleet in 2024, with the company now taking advantage of strong secondhand values to realise a sizeable return. The disposal marks another profitable exit from the 12-ship Avance Gas fleet acquired in August 2024 for $1.05bn in cash, shares and assumed debt. In July, BW LPG agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,000 cu m BW Levant , another vessel from the Avance transaction, with expected net cash proceeds of $38m and a book gain of around $17m. The two deals are set to generate combined book gains of approximately $54m and net cash proceeds of $142m. The latest sale comes amid a broader fleet renewal drive at BW LPG. Its 52%-owned Indian subsidiary has also been selling older VLGCs, most recently agreeing to dispose of the 2008-built BW Loyalty for a price in the low-$80m range, with an expected gain of $52m. At the other end of the fleet, BW LPG has committed around $940m to eight 90,000 cu m panamax VLGC newbuildings at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, scheduled for delivery between 2029 and 2030. The Mark Young-led company said it had conditionally allocated 108.5m shares at NOK17.44 ($1.83) apiece, taking up the full $25m over-allotment on top of its original $175m fundraising target. The transaction comprises 95m new shares raising approximately $174m for Cetus, alongside 13.5m existing shares borrowed from major shareholder Pacific Transportation Asia (PTA) to cover the over-allotment. Together with DNB Asset Management, the four investors had indicated interest in subscribing for a combined $106.5m. Cetus has not disclosed their final individual allocations. The proceeds should help fund Cetus’s acquisition of 13 handysize and ultramax bulkers from Hong Kong-listed Seacon Shipping Group, along with Syngrace, which holds contracts for three additional handysize newbuildings. The transaction involves approximately $72.5m in cash and the issuance of 37.3m Cetus shares to Seacon. The fresh capital will also support newbuilding payments, fleet deleveraging and working capital requirements. Following completion of the fleet acquisition and a planned vessel sale, Cetus said it expects to operate 42 ships, comprising 34 vessels on the water and eight newbuildings scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. The company is targeting November 18 for its first day of trading on Euronext Growth Oslo, subject to regulatory approvals and completion of the Seacon transaction. Cetus has also left the door open for a move to the main Oslo Børs list within 12 months of its debut. The vessels operate under a mix of Russian, Panamanian, Sierra Leonean and Djiboutian flags, according to the official sanctions notice. The restrictions prohibit the specified ships from accessing British ports and impose controls on chartering and operating them. They also restrict the provision of services including ship finance, broking, technical assistance and crewing, subject to applicable exceptions and licensing arrangements. The corporate additions extend the crackdown beyond individual ships. Dubai-based Forteza Trading, Patera and Novus Energy have been designated, with British authorities specifically linking Novus Energy to dealings involving vessels already subject to UK restrictions. Russian petrochemical producer Sibur and coal groups SUEK and Kuzbassrazrezugol also feature in the latest package. The move brings all ten of Russia’s largest oil producers under British sanctions following the inclusion of Slavneft. The government announced the measures during the European Political Community summit in Dublin, where pressure on Russian energy revenues formed part of discussions on Ukraine. Britain has been steadily expanding its maritime restrictions this year, including sanctions against six ships in August and an earlier package targeting Russia’s developing LNG shadow fleet.
